genZNote: Mold in the environment, yeast once it's inside a macrophage — thermal dimorphism as a survival strategy.

morphology.shape: Dimorphic: mold (mycelial) form in the environment/at room temperature, small oval yeast form at body temperature
morphology.size: Yeast form ~2-4 µm; tuberculate macroconidia ~8-14 µm in the mold form
morphology.notes: Despite the species name, it does not have a true polysaccharide capsule — the name is a historical misnomer

habitat.naturalHabitat: Soil enriched with bird or bat droppings
habitat.hostAssociation: Environmental saprophyte; facultative intracellular pathogen within macrophages during infection
habitat.environmentalOccurrence: Endemic to the Ohio and Mississippi River valleys in North America, and other river valley regions worldwide; associated with caves, chicken coops, and bird roosts
habitat.reservoir: Soil contaminated with bird or bat guano

microscopy.stain: Giemsa or methenamine silver stain of tissue/bone marrow; lactophenol cotton blue for mold form
microscopy.appearance: Small oval intracellular yeasts within macrophages in tissue; tuberculate (spiny) macroconidia in the mold form on culture

culture.media: Sabouraud dextrose agar (mold form at 25-30°C); brain-heart infusion blood agar (yeast form at 37°C)
culture.growthCharacteristics: Slow growing — mold form may take 2-4 weeks to develop
culture.colonyMorphology: White to buff, cottony mold colonies at room temperature; smooth, moist, cream-colored yeast colonies at 37°C

identificationClues: Thermal dimorphism — mold at room temperature, yeast at 37°C
Small intracellular yeast forms seen within macrophages on tissue biopsy or bone marrow
Tuberculate (spiny-walled) macroconidia characteristic of the mold form
Urine/serum Histoplasma antigen test is a rapid, sensitive diagnostic tool
Exposure history to bird/bat droppings, caves, or endemic river valley regions

diseases: Pulmonary histoplasmosis (often self-limited in immunocompetent hosts)
Progressive disseminated histoplasmosis (in immunocompromised hosts, e.g. advanced HIV)
clinicalImportance.transmission: Inhalation of microconidia from disturbed soil contaminated with bird or bat droppings (e.g. spelunking, construction, demolition)
clinicalImportance.epidemiology: Endemic to the Ohio and Mississippi River valleys and other river valley regions globally; a major AIDS-defining opportunistic infection in endemic areas
clinicalImportance.labSignificance: Urine antigen testing is faster and more sensitive than culture, which can take weeks due to slow mold growth

examFacts.keyBiochemicalReaction: Not applicable — identified by thermal dimorphism and antigen testing
examFacts.importantTest: Urine/serum Histoplasma antigen test; tissue biopsy showing intracellular yeast in macrophages
examFacts.distinguishingFeature: Thermal dimorphism with tuberculate macroconidia in the mold phase and small intracellular yeasts in tissue
